paper_title: From Rewarding What Models Say to How They Think: Attention Process Reward Model for LLM Reinforcement Learning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become an important component in large language models (LLMs). However, existing RL approaches focus on final outputs or textual solution trajectories, leading to coarse-grained rewards and unreliable reasoning. Such paradigms focus mainly on what the model outputs while overlooking how the model internally reasons. Therefore, can we reward how a model thinks internally rather than merely what it says? We first reveal the problem of textual reward aliasing in existing reward modeling approaches. Motivated by this, we propose the Attention Process Reward Model (APRM), which assigns internal rewards based on hidden states and attention maps to capture high-quality reasoning patterns. With only approximately 46M parameters, APRM is trained using ranking and counterfactual objectives, and its reward guides RL optimization while being periodically updated to handle distribution shifts. Integrated with representative RL methods, APRM achieved an average pass@8 gain of 2.88\%. Our results demonstrate the promise of incorporating internal reasoning signals into RL for LLMs.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become an important component in large language models (LLMs). However, existing RL approaches focus on final outputs or textual solution trajectories, leading to coarse-grained rewards and unreliable reasoning. Such paradigms focus mainly on what the model outputs while overlooking how the model internally reasons. Therefore, can we reward how model thinks internally rather than merely what it says? We first reveal the problem of textual reward aliasing in existing reward modeling approaches. Motivated by this, we propose the Attention Process Reward Model (APRM), which assigns internal rewards based on hidden states and attention maps to capture highquality reasoning patterns. With only approximately 46M parameters, APRM is trained using ranking and counterfactual objectives, and its reward guides RL optimization while being periodically updated to handle distribution shifts. Integrated with representative RL methods, APRM achieved an average pass@8 gain of 2.88%. Our results demonstrate the promise of incorporating internal reasoning signals into RL for LLMs.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: In recent years, large language models (LLMs) (Zhao et al., 2023; Chang et al., 2024; Vaswani et al., 2017) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in complex reasoning tasks (Wang et al., 2024; Plaat et al., 2025). Reinforcement learning (RL) has consequently become an important approach for improving reasoning ability during the post-training stage (Cao et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025). Existing RL approaches for reasoning typically employ outcome reward models (ORMs) (Zhong et al., 2025) and process reward models (PRMs) (Xi et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2024). ORMs reward final-answer correctness, which is scalable but provides only sparse outcome-level feedback and cannot identify which reasoning steps contribute to success or failure. PRMs provide denser supervision by scoring intermediate Chain-of-Thought (CoT) steps, but they rely on Figure 1: Comparison of outcome rewards, textual process rewards, and APRM. 1 natural-language rationales that are costly to annotate. Moreover, existing reward models supervise only externalized reasoning traces. However, reasoning in LLMs is fundamentally latent (Chen et al., 2025; Barez et al., 2025). The internal computation that produces textual trajectory is not directly observable from the trajectory itself. Therefore, textual reward supervision may suffer from process aliasing, where distinct internal reasoning processes induce indistinguishable textual outputs and consequently receive identical rewards. Therefore, question arises: Can we reward how model thinks internally, rather than merely what it says? Mechanistic interpretability studies reveal structured information routing and interpretable computations in attention components (Lan et al., 2024; Merullo et al., 2024; Kissane et al., 2024; Nam et al., 2026), so we use attention-derived signals as partial window into internal computation, extending reward modeling from what models say toward how they think. We first theoretically show that textual reward supervision is fundamentally under-observed. Distinct internal reasoning processes may collapse to indistinguishable textual trajectories and consequently receive identical rewards, phenomenon we term textual reward aliasing. Motivated by this view, we propose the Attention Process Reward Model (APRM), as shown in Figure 1. The APRM is built upon an Attention-Fused Concept Pooler and an Edge-Biased Graph Attention Network (GAT) (Veliˇckovic et al., 2017). APRM directly evaluates hidden states and attention maps from the reasoning process to produce internal process rewards. We use APRM in two stages. During cold-start, APRM uses positive and negative reasoning trajectories with ranking and counterfactual losses to learn preferences over internal reasoning processes. During RL, APRM reshapes the task reward so that policy optimization is guided by both outcomes and internal attention quality. Through systematic analysis of APRM, we obtain three key findings: (1) Positive and negative trajectories exhibit systematic structural differences in the APRM concept-attention space. (2) APRM captures meaningful attention-derived signals and is sensitive to counterfactual attention perturbations. (3) APRM is not proxy for existing metrics. It exhibits length-decoupling behavior and captures complementary process-quality information beyond existing reward supervision. We further validate APRM by integrating it with representative RL methods. As lightweight plug-in module with only approximately 46M parameters, APRM consistently improves avg@8 and pass@8, yielding an average pass@8 gain of 2.88%. Interestingly, APRM also encourages more efficient reasoning behaviors, with tendency toward shorter reasoning trajectories while maintaining or improving performance. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We reveal the phenomenon of the textual reward aliasing problem and demonstrate the information gain of using internal signals as rewards. We propose APRM, lightweight reward model with approximately 46M parameters that evaluates reasoning trajectories using attention-derived internal signals. We systematically analyze the properties of APRM and further validate its effectiveness on downstream reinforcement learning tasks.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP Datasets. We conduct experiments on four widely used reasoning benchmarks, including AIME2025, AMC, MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2024), and OlympiadBench (He et al., 2024). For training, we construct unified dataset of 10K samples by randomly mixing problems from DAPO-17k (Yu et al., 2026) and MATH level 3 5 Figure 4: Stratified Pearson correlations between APRM scores and proxy quality signals within correct and incorrect samples on Qwen3-1.7b-Base and Qwen3-4b-Base backbones. to 5 (Hendrycks et al., 2021). To reduce the impact of randomness, we report both average@8 and pass@8 as the primary evaluation metrics. Baselines. We compare our method against several representative RL and PRM methods, including GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), GPG (Chu et al., 2025), GMPO (Zhao et al., 2025), GSPO (Zheng et al., 2025a), and FAPO (Ding et al., 2025). We adopt Qwen3-1.7b-Base and Qwen3-4b-Base (Yang et al., 2025) as the backbone models for all methods. For the APRM training, we set λrank = 1.0, λcf = 0.05, mrk = mcf = 0.2. We adopt the Verl framework to RL, and the maximum prompt length is 512 tokens. For Qwen3-1.7b-Base, the maximum response length is set to 4096 with β = 0.3. For Qwen3-4b-Base, the maximum response length is set to 3072 with β = 0.1. In addition, APRM is lightweight, introducing only about 46M additional parameters. More details about hyperparameters are shown in Appendix D. 4.2 EVALUATIONS AND ANALYSIS OF APRM Table 1: Attention shuffle robustness analysis of APRM. To assess whether APRM captures attention-derived process information, we randomly shuffle attention summaries while keeping hidden states fixed. We report the median generated token length. The results are summarized in Table 4. Detailed results and analysis are shown in Appendix E. APRM optimizes the models reasoning patterns, which may affect the output length differently across various methods. Overall, however, it exhibits tendency to produce more concise responses. The largest overall decrease is observed for GPG on Qwen3-4b-Base (-17.08%), suggesting that APRM helps the model adapt its token budget to problem difficulty during internal deliberation. Table 3 studies the effect of the β on the final advantage. moderate value performs best overall, with β = 0.3 achieving the strongest avg@8 on AIME2025 and AMC, as well as the highest pass@8 on MATH500. Smaller values underuse the process signal, while larger values can overemphasize APRM and weaken the outcome reward. 4.3.3 GENERALIZATION EXPERIMENTS To further evaluate the generalizability of APRM, we conduct two additional experiments on Qwen3.5-2B instruct and code generation. The cold-start APRM achieves pairwise ranking accuracy of 91.93%. For cross-task validation, we extend APRM to code generation using 3,000 problems from DeepCoder-PreviewDataset. The code-domain cold-start APRM achieves pairwise ranking accuracy of 75.56%. As shown in Table 5, on mathematical reasoning, DAPO+APRM improves the average Avg@8 and Pass@8 by 1.34 and 4.78 percentage points, respectively. On code generation, it achieves gains of 1.64 and 2.96 percentage points, respectively. These results demonstrate that APRM generalizes across instruction-tuned models and task domains, supporting its potential as general-purpose internal process reward model.

Following this direction, GPG (Chu et al., 2025) revisits vanilla policy gradient and directly optimizes the original RL objective without relying on surrogate losses; GSPO (Zheng et al., 2025a) moves policy optimization from token-level importance ratios to sequence-level likelihood ratios; and GMPO (Zhao et al., 2025) introduces geometric-mean objective to reduce sensitivity to outlier rewards and extreme importance ratios. Another line of work focuses on designing richer process reward signals to address the sparsity of outcome supervision (Zhang et al., 2024; Setlur et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2024). These methods have shown that process-level supervision can substantially improve mathematical reasoning. RLAnything (Wang et al., 2026) proposes dynamic closed-loop RL framework that jointly evolves the environment, policy, and reward model. However, these approaches still primarily define rewards over external outcomes, textual trajectories, or task-level interactions, leaving model-internal reasoning signals largely unexplored. 5.2 ATTENTION MECHANISM IN RL Recent circuit analysis studies have shown that attention-based sub-circuits contribute to and implement interpretable model behaviors (Lan et al., 2024; Merullo et al., 2024). Furthermore, causal intervention methods have demonstrated that certain attention heads have identifiable functional contributions to model outputs (Kissane et al., 2024; Nam et al., 2026). These findings suggest that attention patterns are not merely superficial statistical correlations with model outputs, but can provide partial observations of the internal computation underlying model behavior. TCRM (Nikulkov, 2026) exploits causal attention with temporal regularization for smooth token-level values. Extending beyond linear reasoning, GraphPRM (Peng et al., 2025) models trajectories as graphs with GAT-based dependency learning for error localization. To mitigate PRM-induced verbosity and length bias, CoLD (Zheng et al., 2025b) uses feature perturbation to force uniform self-attention distribution in the bias estimator, precisely filtering out the PRMs length bias via counterfactual inference. Multilingual PRM (Wang et al., 2025) further aligns attention representations across languages for robust multilingual policies. Unlike reward-centric methods, RAL (Li et al., 2026) directly optimizes self-attention distributions as the RL policy itself. Unlike prior work, APRM is the first to directly supervise models internal signals, scoring attention and hidden states directly in the latent space.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We reveal textual reward aliasing, where identical or similar external trajectories may conceal distinct internal reasoning processes and thus receive indistinguishable rewards. To address this, we propose APRM, lightweight internal process reward model with 46M parameters that scores hidden-state and attention-based reasoning signals. Integrated with existing RL algorithms, APRM provides complementary supervision and consistently improves reasoning performance. Interestingly, APRM also encourages more efficient reasoning behaviors, with tendency toward shorter reasoning trajectories while maintaining or improving performance. These results suggest broader direction for RL that rewards not only what models say but also how they think.

sections.title: A FUTURE WORK
sections.content: Exploring More Effective Reward Architectures. Although our ablation studies validate the contributions of attention-based concept pooling and GAT, the optimal architecture for internal process reward modeling remains an open question. Future work could explore alternative graph architectures, more expressive concept interactions, and richer internal representations beyond the current hidden states and attention maps. systematic investigation of these architectural choices may further improve the effectiveness and efficiency of internal reward modeling. Advanced Reward Integration Strategies. In this work, we adopt simple additive formulation with fixed coefficient to incorporate APRM into existing RL algorithms, allowing us to isolate the contribution of internal process rewards. However, more sophisticated integration strategies may further exploit the complementary information provided by internal and external reward signals.

sections.title: B PROMPT DETAILS
sections.content: For the LLM-as-judge evaluation, we use GLM-5.1 to assess the process quality of APRM-scored reasoning samples. Each judged instance contains the original math question, the gold final answer, the model-generated solution, and binary correctness flag. The judge is instructed to evaluate reasoning quality rather than final-answer correctness, and returns integer scores from 0 to 10 on five dimensions: reasoning coherence, conciseness, redundancy, step validity, and overall process quality. We use deterministic decoding with temperature 0 and top-p 1.0, and require the judge to output JSON object with the five scores and brief rationale. The returned scores are parsed, clipped to the range [0, 10], and stored together with the corresponding APRM score for correlation analysis. The prompt we use is as follows: Teacher LLMs System Prompt You are an expert evaluator for mathematical reasoning quality. You will be given: 1. math question 2. The gold final answer 3. model-generated solution 4. Whether the final answer is correct Your job is to evaluate the reasoning process quality of the model-generated solution, not just the final answer correctness. Please score the solution on the following five dimensions, each on an integer scale from 0 to 10: 1. reasoning_coherence - Does the reasoning flow logically from step to step? - Are the transitions natural and internally faithful to the line of thought? - High score: coherent, well-connected reasoning chain. - Low score: abrupt jumps, contradictions, disconnected reasoning. 2. conciseness - Does the solution use an efficient amount of text to communicate the reasoning? - High score: compact, information-dense, little unnecessary verbosity. - Low score: overly long, bloated, too much unnecessary explanation. 3. redundancy - How much repetitive or unnecessary repetition is present? - High score: little repetition, low redundancy. - Low score: repetitive statements, circular restatements, duplicated work. 4. step_validity - Are the intermediate reasoning steps mathematically valid and locally sound? - High score: most steps are valid and justified. - Low score: frequent invalid transformations, unsupported claims, local mathematical errors. 5. overall_process_quality - Overall quality of the reasoning process, considering the above dimensions together. - High score: strong reasoning process even if the final answer is wrong due to small slip. - Low score: poor reasoning process even if the final answer happens to be correct by luck. Important instructions: - Do not simply map final correctness to high score. correct answer with poor reasoning can still score low. - Do not punish small final arithmetic slip too harshly if the process is otherwise strong. - Focus on the reasoning process quality, not surface style alone. - Return only single JSON object, with no markdown fences and no extra text. - All scores must be integers between 0 and 10. Return this JSON schema exactly: { "reasoning_coherence": 0, "conciseness": 0, 14 "redundancy": 0, "step_validity": 0, "overall_process_quality": 0, "brief_rationale": "" } The "brief_rationale" should be short English explanation in 1 to 3 sentences summarizing the judgment.

sections.title: C ADDITIONAL APRM CASE STUDIES
sections.content: Due to space limitations in the main text, we provide additional APRM case studies in the appendix. These examples further illustrate that APRM does not simply act as proxy for response length, but assigns scores according to the structure and reliability of the reasoning process. In Figure 8, APRM assigns higher score to the rollout that correctly uses the algebraic property of the nonreal cubic root and derives the final value, while the lower-scored rollout reaches an incorrect result despite presenting compact derivation. In Figure 9, the higher-scored rollout applies the appropriate trigonometric relation and obtains the correct side length, whereas the lower-scored rollout uses an incorrect secant-based approximation and produces wrong answer. Figure 10 shows base-conversion problem where APRM favors the solution with more faithful conversion and digit-sum computation over shorter but incorrect trajectory. Overall, these cases show that APRM scores are sensitive to reasoning validity and structural correctness rather than verbosity. Short responses can still receive low scores when their reasoning is flawed.

We train APRM for 5 epochs using AdamW with learning rate 1 104, weight decay 1 102, cosine learning-rate scheduling, and warmup ratio of 0.05. D.4 ABLATION ON ATTENTION AND GRAPH MODELING To investigate the respective contributions of attention-derived representations and graph modeling, we conduct additional architectural ablations on Qwen3.5-2B across mathematical reasoning and code generation. Specifically, we compare the full APRM with two variants: (1) APRM w/o GAT, which removes graph propagation, and (2) Hidden MLP, which uses hidden-state representations without attention-based concept modeling. All variants are trained under identical data and training configurations, with nearly matched trainable parameter counts to minimize the influence of model capacity. APRM APRM w/o GAT Hidden MLP 44.251M 44.251M 44.128M 75.56% 75.31% 71.42% 91.93% 90.95% 84.39% As shown in Table 7, attention-based concept modeling provides substantial improvements over the hiddenstate-only MLP, increasing ranking accuracy by 4.14 and 6.56 percentage points on code generation and mathematics, respectively. Incorporating GAT further improves accuracy by 0.25 and 0.98 percentage points, indicating modest additional benefit from modeling concept-level dependencies. Overall, these results highlight the importance of attention-derived representations in APRM, while suggesting that graph-based relational modeling provides complementary benefits. Nevertheless, identifying the optimal architecture for internal process reward modeling remains an open direction for future research. 19 D.5 RL TRAINING DETAILS We use the verl framework as the training backbone for all reinforcement learning experiments. For each RL algorithm, including GRPO, GPG, GSPO, GMPO, and FAPO, we keep the default hyperparameters provided by its verl implementation unless otherwise specified. To ensure fair comparison, each baseline and its APRM-enhanced variant use the same GPU configuration, batch size, and training schedule. Due to GPU computational constraints, we set the per-GPU batch size to 6. For experiments run on 4 GPUs, the global batch size is 48 and the model is trained for 200 steps. For experiments run on 2 GPUs, the global batch size is 24 and the model is trained for 400 steps. This keeps the total number of training samples approximately aligned across different settings. When comparing an RL method with and without APRM, all default RL hyperparameters and hardware settings are kept unchanged, except for the additional APRM-related hyperparameters introduced by our method. For APRM-enhanced RL, the APRM advantage coefficient is denoted by β. We use β = 0.3 for Qwen3-1.7b-Base and β = 0.1 for Qwen3-4b-Base. As an exception, for GSPO we use β = 0.2.

sections.title: E DETAILED ANALYSIS OF RESPONSE LENGTH
sections.content: Table 8 reports the median response length across benchmarks, separated by method, model scale, and correctness. The comparison suggests that APRM does not impose fixed length preference. Instead, its effect depends on the underlying RL algorithm and model scale. For GPG, APRM consistently shortens responses. The reduction is mild on Qwen3-1.7b-Base, with the overall average length decreasing by 3.03%, and becomes more pronounced on Qwen3-4b-Base, where the overall average length decreases by 17.08%. similar pattern appears for GRPO on Qwen3-4b-Base, where APRM reduces the overall response length by 7.95%. These results indicate that APRM often suppresses unnecessarily long reasoning traces, especially for larger backbones. For GRPO on Qwen3-1.7b-Base and GSPO on Qwen3-1.7b-Base, APRM increases the overall response length by 22.25% and 1.63%, respectively. This suggests that APRM changes the models reasoning behavior rather than simply penalizing long outputs. In some cases, it encourages more complete intermediate reasoning when the baseline responses are relatively short. Overall, APRM tends to reduce verbosity in most settings while remaining sensitive to the optimization dynamics of different RL algorithms. This supports the view that APRM is not length proxy, but process-level signal that reshapes reasoning trajectories according to their internal structure and quality.
